rows.label: Concept
rows.text: ## The poem at a glance "All the World's a Stage" is Jaques' famous speech from Shakespeare's *As You Like It* (Act II, Scene vii) — technically drama, treated in the syllabus as a poem, and one of the most extended **extended metaphors** in English: the world is a stage, all people are actors, and a life is a play in seven acts.…

rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
Extended metaphor: life as theatre; the seven ages are seven acts.
Know the stages in order — infant, schoolboy, lover, soldier, justice, pantaloon, second childhood.

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: Trick 3: The last age is the harshest: sans teeth, sans eyes, sans taste, sans everything — the repetition 'sans' drives the message of decline; quote it.  ·  ## The themes worth an essay **The stages of life** — the surface theme, and the exam's favourite: identify the seven ages and their traits. **The predictability of human life** — Jaques implies every life runs the same route; the comfort and the horror are the same fact. **Role-playing and identity** — we are our costumes as much as our selves; the lover is only a lover while the part lasts.…

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: ## The title, defended The speech is known by its first line because the first line *is* the poem: "All the world's a stage" is not a title hung on an argument but the argument itself, stated as fact. A candidate defending it should say exactly that: the title performs the metaphor's confidence — no "perhaps", no "like" — and the certainty is what makes the seven ages follow so obediently.  ·  ## How NEB asks it **"List the seven ages of man with one trait each." (7 marks)** — infant (helpless), schoolboy (unwilling), lover (sentimental), soldier (ambitious), justice (pompous), pantaloon (shrinking), second childhood (dependent). Learn them as a walk, not a list.…

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: Q. List the seven ages of man. (3 marks) — infant, schoolboy, lover, soldier, justice, pantaloon, second childhood.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: Q. List the seven ages of man. (3 marks) — infant, schoolboy, lover, soldier, justice, pantaloon, second childhood.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: ## Reading it closely, age by age **The opening metaphor** sets the rules: "All the world's a stage, and all the men and women merely players." *Merely* is the knife in the sentence — not just players, but *only* players: our roles are assigned, our exits not ours to schedule.…  ·  ## The devices, with evidence - **Extended metaphor** — the master device: world = stage, life = play, and every detail obedient to it (entrances, exits, parts, acts). - **Simile** — "creeps like snail", "sighs like furnace", "bearded like the pard": each age given an animal or an object that *is* its temperament. - **Imagery** — theatrical and bodily at once: satchels, beards, round bellies, slippers, hose.…

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Trick 1: The extended metaphor: life = drama, people = actors, God = playwright — state the controlling metaphor before anything else.  ·  Trick 2: The seven ages in order: infant, schoolboy, lover, soldier, justice, pantaloon (old man), second childhood — memorise the list; sequencing questions are guaranteed.

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: Q. What is the message of the poem? (2 marks) — life is a predictable performance from entry to exit; humans merely play their parts.
